name: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
title: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
answer: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of finding and executing a trade path through one or more on-chain liquidity pools to get a desired asset at a better effective price than a single pool would offer. It covers order splitting, multi-hop paths, and the choice between different pool designs such as constant product, stable swaps, and concentrated liquidity. The scope includes both simple swaps and more complex strategies that route across several chains or layer 2 networks. It sits in crypto markets and decentralised finance, where the router is often a smart contract or an off-chain service that submits transactions.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of finding and executing a trade path through one or more on-chain liquidity pools to get a desired asset at a better effective price than a single pool would offer. It covers order splitting, multi-hop paths, and the choice between different pool designs such as constant product, stable swaps, and concentrated liquidity. The scope includes both simple swaps and more complex strategies that route across several chains or layer 2 networks. It sits in crypto markets and decentralised finance, where the router is often a smart contract or an off-chain service that submits transactions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on public blockchains and their virtual machines, most commonly Ethereum and EVM-compatible networks, plus layer 2 rollups and sidechains. Routers depend on RPC nodes, block explorers, and indexers to read pool reserves, tick data, and recent trades. They also rely on price oracles and mempool monitoring to estimate slippage, gas costs, and competing transactions. Execution happens through signed transactions that call pool contracts, with nonce management and gas bidding handled by the router or a wallet.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A router typically starts with a graph of pools and tokens, then searches for paths that minimise the effective price after fees, slippage, and gas. It may split a single order across several pools or hops to reduce price impact, and it simulates the result against current state before submitting. Many routers use off-chain computation for pathfinding and on-chain contracts for settlement, sometimes with a solver or auction mechanism. The method also includes handling failed transactions, front-running, and sandwich attacks by adjusting slippage tolerance or using private transaction channels.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on smart contract correctness, liquidity provenance, and the legal status of the tokens being routed. A router can inherit bugs from the pools it touches, and it can expose users to impermanent loss, oracle manipulation, and MEV extraction. Provenance matters because a pool's liquidity may come from unknown or sanctioned sources, and the router may not screen for that. Regulatory treatment of DeFi routing varies by jurisdiction, and compliance pages on this site track the shifting rules.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward intent-based routing, where a user states a desired outcome and competing solvers find the best path across many venues. Cross-chain routing and account abstraction are making the user experience less dependent on manual network and gas choices. AI and machine learning are being applied to pathfinding, slippage prediction, and MEV detection, though the core problem remains a search over a changing graph. Over time, routing may become more modular, with shared solvers and standardised settlement layers, but the risks of smart contract failure and market manipulation will not disappear.
